3.0.s.en: (1) Warning against the teaching of false teachers

3.0.0.en: Finally: in the original Greek, "as for the rest of the discourse."

3.0.1.en: Safe: it protects you and keeps you secure.

3.0.2.en: The Apostle calls them to spiritual joy, because the mark of the Christian life is joy in the many graces of God that He has poured out upon us, and moreover joy gives us strength in our spiritual striving. These two matters, that is, the call to joy and the matter that follows it, which is the warning against the false teachers, St. Paul does not tire of repeating, because it keeps them secure from slipping into believing these teachings.

3.1.0.en: Beware: the Greek word here has the original meaning "always watch out for and avoid." The concision: he means the false teachers, who are converts from a Jewish background and who proclaim the necessity of circumcision for obtaining salvation. Circumcision is called "the concision," that is, the cutting of a part of the body as an outward act without its spiritual meaning.

3.1.1.en: St. Paul called the false teachers dogs because they tear at the body of the Church, causing division and working against the Gospel, and they proclaim circumcision, which is a cutting in the flesh only, without its spiritual meaning, which is turning away from sin and which was a type of Baptism.

3.2.0.en: We have no confidence in the flesh: we do not rely on the works of the flesh, that is, the works of the Law, but we live its spiritual meaning in our faith in Christ, in whose salvation we glory.

3.2.1.en: For we Christians live the true circumcision, that is, the circumcision of the heart by the Spirit, which is turning away from evil, and we obey the Lord in the Church and do not rely on bodily circumcision and the other ordinances of the Law as means of justification.

3.2.2.en: Remain firm in the Church and in her spiritual practices and teachings, and then you will not be exposed to slipping into the strange teachings proclaimed by those who have left the Church, because your habit of the spiritual life with Christ gladdens your heart with it and will make you discover and reject anything foreign to it, lest it separate you from your enjoyment of this joy.

3.3.s.en: (2) Glorying in Christ and not in the Law

3.3.0.en: In the following verses the Apostle Paul mentions seven advantages he had in Judaism that make him surpass the standing of others who glory in the ordinances of the Law. If those Jews think they are something because of their practice of those ordinances, he has advantages that surpass them all.

3.4.0.en: Circumcised the eighth day: St. Paul's being circumcised on the eighth day is proof that he was born in the Jewish religion and was not an outsider to it, because proselytes are circumcised on the day they enter the Jewish faith; of the stock of Israel: this confirms the purity of his lineage.

3.4.1.en: Of the tribe of Benjamin: which had a special standing in Israel, for Benjamin is the only son of Jacob who was born in the Promised Land, and his tribe also remained attached to the tribe of Judah after the division, that is, holding fast to worship in the temple at Jerusalem.

3.4.2.en: A Hebrew: born of Hebrew parents, and he kept the Hebrew tongue although he was born in a Gentile land.

3.4.3.en: Hebrews: that is, the descendants of Abraham, because Eber was one of the forefathers of Abraham (Gen 11:16), and Abraham is called the Hebrew because he crossed the river and left his kindred and his family, as God told him, to live in the land of Canaan and worship Him there (Acts 7:2). A Pharisee: he learned and was trained in the stricter Pharisaic school, so his duty was to keep the details of the Law.

3.4.4.en: Paul declares that he is truly a Jew like all other Jews, so he affirms his circumcision and clarifies his lineage, and even his superiority, since he was among those strict in holding to the Law, that is, a Pharisee.

3.5.0.en: Before Paul's faith in Christ, his chief occupation was the destruction of the Church and the persecution of Christians, and he was very strict in carrying out the commandments of the Law, so that he did not violate its teachings in anything throughout his former life, and no one can blame him for any shortcoming on his part.

3.6.0.en: All the previous advantages, which many of the Jews regard as great gains, Paul considered to be of no benefit and as nothing if they hindered him from knowing Christ.

3.7.0.en: What St. Paul lost by leaving the Jewish religion when he believed in Christ, he considered as nothing compared with what he gained, namely his new life in the Christian faith.

3.8.0.en: My union with Christ in the Church gives me security, and I obtain salvation by my sonship to her, whereas outside the Church is loss and eternal perdition, because the Law was unable to grant man righteousness; man cannot be justified by himself, but by faith in Christ he arrives at the state of righteousness and holiness.

3.8.1.en: All that the world may give us does not satisfy our souls, but the knowledge of Christ gives rest to our hearts and grants us a peace that surpasses all understanding. Therefore may we give priority in our time to God before the preoccupations of the world and its comfort and its pleasures, for they are all passing and do not satisfy our souls.

3.9.0.en: St. Paul's rejection of all the previous advantages was for the sake of knowing Christ truly, and of grasping the victory He achieved over all the powers of evil when He raised Himself by His divine power after the death of the Cross, and drew him up from the death of sin to the life of fellowship with Him, accepting every suffering the world imposes on him, to share with the Lord Jesus His sufferings for the sake of righteousness, and he longs for martyrdom, being conformed to His death.

3.10.0.en: The Apostle hopes to rise on the great day of judgment in the resurrection of the righteous to eternal life. And he highlights here the difficulty of attaining this and that it requires striving and vigilance.

3.11.0.en: The Apostle wanted to teach us that as long as we are in the body we must strive toward perfection until the last breath. He expresses here clearly a life of pursuit and striving until we reach salvation and eternal life, that blessed end for which the Lord Christ sought him and turned him from a persecutor of the Church into a great apostle defending the Christian faith.

3.12.0.en: After St. Paul considers what he has done during his life, he sees that he has not yet reached the required level. Much growth is still needed, so the only thing he sets as the foundation of his present striving is to refuse to look at the past of his life with its errors, and to concentrate his thoughts and his effort on his responsibility toward his righteousness and his Church.

3.13.1.en: The goal for which he strives is God's holy calling for the salvation of all, and his being crowned with the crown of glory that the just Judge will grant him on that day.

3.13.2.en: To the degree that you feel the greatness of being with God and the glory of the Kingdom, you hold fast to striving in the spiritual life and reject every sin by repentance, and you even cut off all sources of evil and persevere in your striving by the help of God, who supports you and encourages you until you reach your goal.

3.14.0.en: This: that is, the constant pursuit in spiritual striving.

3.14.1.en: Perfect: those who are pursuing perfection.

3.14.2.en: Let us who are spiritually mature have this mind, which is the mind of Christ. But if some of you are occupied with another mind contrary to this and are exposed to deviations on the way, God will reveal the truth to you by His Spirit who dwells in you.

3.15.0.en: Whereto we have already attained: our previous spiritual practice of prayers, fasts and various acts of worship. Rule: the spiritual order by which we worship God and serve Him.

3.15.1.en: Mind the same thing: the importance of continuing in spiritual striving.

3.15.2.en: What we practiced of spiritual striving in our past spiritual life, let us persevere in it, assured of the importance of the constant pursuit toward the Kingdom.

3.16.s.en: (4) The end of the wicked and the righteous

3.16.0.en: Because the Apostle imitates Christ in his life, he asks the Philippians to imitate him also in his life and conduct, and also to imitate their spiritual guides, who are an example to them.

3.17.0.en: Walk: they behave in evil and strange heresies.

3.17.1.en: The enemies of the cross of Christ, by their deviant thoughts, lead people astray from the Savior Christ who was crucified for our redemption.

3.17.2.en: As for these who followed the strange teachings and whom the Apostle warned against being influenced by their opinions, he repeats here the warning against them despite his love for them and his weeping over them. The Apostle hates their evils and their sin and not their persons, for he regards them as erring sons.

3.18.0.en: The destiny of these false teachers is eternal destruction, for they are always hastening to satisfy their whims and worldly desires, and they do evil and boast of doing it.

3.19.0.en: But as for us, because our original homeland is heaven, we walk spiritually like the heavenly ones, eagerly expecting the coming of Christ at His Second Coming, and awaiting His promise to save us from the misery of the present world and to let us enjoy His eternal glory.

3.20.0.en: For it is He who will change this weak body of ours, which is subject to sickness, pain and disfigurement and liable to sin and falling, into a glorified body without sin, like His body with which He rose from the dead, for He who was able to conquer death by Himself has the power to give life to our mortal bodies.

3.20.1.en: May we look every day to our goal, which is heaven, so that we walk in a manner worthy of life there, in purity and love for everyone, and always contemplate the life of the angels and the saints in heaven, and seek their intercession and imitate their conduct, so that we taste the earnest of the Kingdom while we are on earth and our longing for it increases. Virtues, steadfastness and giving

4.0.0.en: Therefore, you whom I love and long for, you who are the cause of my joy and the reason for my obtaining the crown with which the Lord will crown me in eternal glory, I ask you to hold fast to the faith of Christ and His commandments.

4.1.0.en: The Apostle asks two women servants in Philippi, "Euodias and Syntyche," to end the disagreements between them so that they may agree on one mind, which is the mind of Christ.

4.2.0.en: True yokefellow: it is thought that he is Luke, who accompanied him (Acts 16:10-17), or Epaphroditus, the writer of this letter (v. 23), or one of Paul's disciples who assisted him in the service of the church of Philippi.

4.2.1.en: Give up your opinion even if it is right, in order to preserve the peace of the ministry, because being upset will cause many to stumble and make you troubled. And take care to reconcile those who differ with one another in order to remove all tension; in this you will be a son of God and a peacemaker.

4.3.s.en: (2) A call to virtues and Christian conduct

4.3.0.en: The Apostle calls for constant joy and repeats his call to rejoice to stress that it is necessary, for nothing in the world can take away the feelings of joy from believers, whatever the circumstances or troubles or tribulations around them, because the source of joy is God who dwells in the heart; but care must be taken that the joy be in Christ and pleasing to Him and not in the manner of the world.

4.4.0.en: The Apostle commands them to adorn themselves with patience and keep away from anger, which means a call to a life of surrender and endurance, and to show this virtue to people not by way of pretense or boasting but so that people may see the virtues in Christianity. Our life on earth is short, and we always expect the Lord's coming to be near, therefore we readily give up many of our material rights and bear patiently with those who wrong us, since our eyes are fixed on the Kingdom and the Second Coming of Christ.

4.5.0.en: He also asks them to cast off from themselves the cares of life and all anxiety, and not to be troubled and confused before trials, but to hold fast to prayer, for it is the only way to true rest and a sure remedy for anxiety, and let them lift up their personal needs in supplication, always accompanied by thanksgiving.

4.6.0.en: The Apostle wishes them the peace of God, who is able to keep their hearts and direct all their thought toward Christ who strengthens them, because however much human wisdom a person attains, he cannot attain such divine peace, which surpasses the level of the human mind.

4.6.1.en: You can enjoy peace and joy, the desire of all people, if your relationship with God is strong, and specifically if you are devoted to prayer, not only at its appointed times in your inner room and in the church, but throughout the day. And if you meet with wrongs from others and the problems of life, place them before God in prayer, confident of His care and His providence, and continue to delight in speaking with Him.

4.7.2.en: In sum, he asks them to practice this daily conduct in their Christian life, holding fast to the truth, that is, being truthful in what belongs to others as in what belongs to themselves. And let their thoughts be occupied with all that is true in the sight of God and all that is noble and of great worth. And let them follow justice in all their relationships with God and people: with God by keeping His rights, and with people by wronging no one. And let them preserve purity of thought and seek it with all their hearts and do what pleases God and people. And let them have a good reputation and good conduct before everyone, and seek to acquire virtues and perform every deed that deserves praise.

4.8.0.en: He also hopes that they will walk in all that they learned and heard from him about the life of holiness and saw him doing as well. And the God of peace, whom He grants to them, will be with them and help them in their spiritual striving to acquire these virtues.

4.9.s.en: (3) His thanks to them for their gifts and their reward

4.9.0.en: The Apostle expresses his joy and thanks to the Lord and to them, likening their work for him to a tree blossoming a second time and putting forth new leaves. For the church of Philippi had not been able to send him material help for a long time because of the difficulty of travel on the roads, and then the Lord allowed them to care for him again after they had waited a long time for an opportunity to do so.

4.10.0.en: What he told them about his joy is not for the material help in itself so much as for their love that appeared in their gifts. For since he became a Christian he learned how to live a life of contentment, satisfaction and sufficiency with what he has.

4.11.0.en: He knows how to live on little and be satisfied with it, and even to keep some of it in reserve. In all the circumstances he faced he is always content in the Lord, whether in hunger or fullness, in abundance of material goods or in their lack, and the secret of this is Christ who dwells in him.

4.12.0.en: For from Christ he draws the strength and ability to face all circumstances and overcome all difficulties.

4.13.0.en: St. Paul appreciates the labor of love of the people of Philippi and thanks them for all that they did and gave as gifts for his sake, since he felt their sharing with him in his affliction during the period of his imprisonment.

4.14.0.en: After St. Paul preached to the people of Philippi and left their province, Macedonia, no church shared with him in giving gifts as they did. And here he magnifies their giving, so he regards them as partners in his ministry.

4.15.0.en: St. Paul does not forget their sending more than once to help him provide for the needs of the ministry, and that was when he was in Thessalonica.

4.16.0.en: All the sincere love they offer is added to their account in the Kingdom. Paul does not want them to think that he is concerned with seeking the gift, but he asks God to reward them with abundant fruit here and in eternity.

4.17.0.en: Their offerings have supplied all his needs and even overflowed beyond the need, and he received from Epaphroditus their gifts, which are with the Lord sacrifices of love, acceptable and of a sweet savor, as was said of the sacrifices of the Old Testament, which were for acceptance and pleasure (Lev 1:9, 13).

4.18.0.en: Therefore he asks the Lord to supply all their needs according to His unlimited riches and by the merits of Jesus Christ, in whom their offerings become pleasing and acceptable to the Father, so that He rewards them in this age and in the age to come.

4.19.0.en: At the close of the letter he gives glory to God our Father forever.

4.19.1.en: How great is Paul's appreciation of the gifts of the people of Philippi. May you show your appreciation for what others do toward you, and likewise for everything good in them, for words of encouragement are needed by all people, old and young, especially if you are going to have to blame someone, you must begin your words to him with encouragement and praise.

4.20.0.en: The Apostle concludes his letter by presenting his greetings to every believer in the church of Philippi, and he sends to the people of Philippi the greetings of his fellow workers in the ministry and his assistants in the preaching in Rome.

4.21.0.en: He also sends the greetings of all the members of the Church in Rome and of the members of the imperial guard in Caesar's household, whom the Apostle led to the knowledge of Christ.

4.22.0.en: The Apostle began his letter with grace and ends it also by asking grace for them, grace which is the work of God with the human soul.

4.22.1.en: The last sentence in the letter was written to clarify the place where the letter was written and the person by whom it was sent.

4.22.2.en: How beautiful is the fellowship among the members of the Church in the exchange of greetings, love and good wishes. May we care for fellowship and affection within our family and with our relatives and in the Church, for this gives rest and satisfaction to the soul, as well as good relationships with others.
